Empirical Research Plan  
“Minimum‐Wage Increases and Employment in Contiguous Border Counties, 1990–2006”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy: Difference-in-Differences (two–way fixed effects) supplemented by dynamic “event-study” coefficients.

Rationale  
• The treatment (a state minimum-wage hike) occurs at discrete times and only on one side of a state border.  
• The natural comparison unit is the neighboring county across the border whose labor-market conditions are otherwise highly similar.  
• DID with county-pair fixed effects removes all time-invariant cross-border differences (demographics, industrial mix, geography) while common quarter fixed effects remove nationwide shocks.  
• An event-study version of the model allows us to test the key parallel-trend assumption.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
Wc,t  = log(real effective minimum wage) in county c at quarter t.  
The treatment “dose” is the within-pair difference in Wc,t.

Construction  
ΔWp,t = Wleft,t – Wright,t, where left and right are the two counties in pair p.  
A positive change in ΔWp,t indicates the left-hand county became (or remained) the higher-minimum-wage side.

Control group  
The lower-minimum-wage county in the pair at each t provides the counterfactual for the higher-minimum-wage county. County-pairs with no change in ΔW are implicitly part of the control because β is identified off within-pair changes.

Treatment timing / event date  
Quarter in which the state minimum increases above its neighbor’s. Event time k = 0 is the first quarter when ΔW jumps.

(We do not need an RDD running variable because we are exploiting discrete law changes, not a continuous cutoff.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: In absence of the minimum-wage change, employment in the two sides of a border would have followed the same trajectory.  
Plausibility: Counties share the same local product and labor markets; pre-trend tests and event-study plots can be inspected.

A2. No cross-border spillovers large enough to bias estimates (e.g., restaurants relocating or workers commuting across the border in response to the policy).  
Plausibility: Some spillovers are likely but usually small relative to county employment. We can test for migration of establishments using QCEW counts.

A3. Policy exogeneity conditional on pair fixed effects: The precise timing of state minimum-wage hikes is not driven by idiosyncratic shocks that differentially affect the two counties within a pair.  
Plausibility: While politics matter, the left vs. right county in a pair cannot lobby separately; shocks at the state level affect both sides symmetrically and are absorbed by quarter × state-region FE in robustness checks.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Cross-border spillovers  
• Test for changes in employment on the low-wage side after the neighbor’s hike.  
• Use larger geographic controls (e.g., 2-county “rings”) to see if results dissipate.  
• Bound the bias by assuming worst-case spillovers and re-estimating.

T2. Differential time-varying shocks (e.g., local plant opening, hurricane, casino legalization)  
• Add pair-specific linear or quadratic trends.  
• Control for county-level unemployment, population, and private-employment growth.  
• Drop observations with major natural disasters (FEMA data).

T3. Endogenous state policy tied to regional cycles  
• Include census-division-by-quarter fixed effects to soak up regional macro trends.  
• Instrument log minimum wage with a “placebo” statutory minimum (what the state law would have been if legislators had only indexed by inflation)—a robustness IV that is predetermined.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# Load packages ---------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)       # high-dimensional FE regressions
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load data ----------------------------------------------------
qwi  <- fread("qwi_restaurants_1990_2006.csv")   # county-quarter obs
mw   <- fread("state_min_wage_1990_2006.csv")    # state-quarter
pairs<- fread("contiguous_county_pairs.csv")      # mapping of counties to pairs

# 2. Merge & construct variables ---------------------------------
setkey(qwi, state_fips, county_fips, quarter)
setkey(mw,    state_fips, quarter)

# attach minimum-wage to each county-quarter
qwi <- mw[qwi]

# merge county-pair identifier
setkey(pairs, state_fips, county_fips)
qwi  <- pairs[qwi]

# outcome
qwi[, ln_emp := log(restaurants_emp)]

# real minimum wage (deflate by CPI-U; assume cpi variable present)
qwi[, ln_mw := log(min_wage / cpi)]

# within-pair mean-centered treatment (demean by pair × quarter)
qwi[, ln_mw_pair_mean := mean(ln_mw), by = .(pair_id, quarter)]
qwi[, ln_mw_dev       := ln_mw - ln_mw_pair_mean]

# 3. Main DID regression -----------------------------------------
did_main <- feols(ln_emp ~ ln_mw_dev | pair_id + quarter,
                  data = qwi,
                  cluster = ~pair_id)

summary(did_main)

# 4. Event-study --------------------------------------------------
# define event time (k = -12…+12) relative to first minimum-wage hike in the pair
qwi[, hike_date  := min(quarter[ln_mw_dev > 0]), by = pair_id]
qwi[, event_time := quarter - hike_date]

# keep balanced window
qwi_es <- qwi[event_time >= -12 & event_time <= 12]

event <- feols(ln_emp ~ i(event_time, ref = -1) | pair_id + quarter,
               data = qwi_es,
               cluster = ~pair_id)

iplot(event)     # built-in fixest plotting of event coefficients

# 5. Robustness: pair-specific trends -----------------------------
did_trend <- feols(ln_emp ~ ln_mw_dev | pair_id + quarter + pair_id[trend],
                   data = qwi,
                   cluster = ~pair_id)

etable(did_main, did_trend, stats = "r2")

# (Additional: replicate on QCEW employment or run IV with statutory index)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Prior from recent empirical and theoretical literature: very small or zero disemployment effect in the restaurant sector.  
Elasticity (β) between −0.05 and 0.00; i.e., a 10 percent minimum-wage hike reduces restaurant employment by at most 0.5 percent and plausibly not at all.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
(1 = satisfied, 0 = questionable)  
C1. No major pre-trend differences ………… 1  
C2. No large spillovers ………………………….. 0  
C3. Stable composition of units ……………. 1  
C4. Treatment exogeneity within pairs ….. 1  
C5. Correct model / functional form …….. 1  

Total = 4 / 5. The most concerning issue is potential cross-border spillovers, which we explicitly test and bound.
